text: Everything built so far — bit-flip, phase-flip, Shor, Steane — is correct and real, but none of it is what actual quantum hardware roadmaps are built around. This lesson explains why the surface code is different, and what it actually costs.

Three properties make it hardware-friendly. First, only nearest-neighbor connectivity is required: every surface-code stabilizer touches just 4 physically neighboring qubits on a 2D grid, matching how real superconducting qubits are actually wired — no long-range connections to the far side of the chip, unlike the Steane code's stabilizers. Second, a comparatively high error threshold: real, achievable physical qubit error rates have a realistic shot at falling below it, which isn't true of every candidate code. Third, low-weight, local stabilizers — every one touches exactly 4 qubits, meaning each round of syndrome extraction only needs short, simple circuits.

These properties come at a real price. Using the verified formula for the rotated surface code, total qubits equals 2 d squared minus 1: at distance 3, that's 17 qubits; distance 5, 49; distance 7, 97; distance 9, 161; distance 11, 241; distance 15, 449. Compare that to the Steane code's flat 7 qubits — the surface code needs dramatically more physical qubits, because its distance is a tunable knob you can push arbitrarily high, not a fixed value like the Steane code's distance of 3.

Leading candidate doesn't mean solved. The surface code is the architecture most real hardware roadmaps are actually building toward, specifically because of those three properties — but running one at the distances genuinely useful fault-tolerant computation needs, hundreds to thousands of physical qubits per logical qubit, times however many logical qubits an algorithm requires, remains a forward-looking engineering target, not something achieved today with current NISQ-era hardware.
Next lesson builds the surface code's actual 2D layout from scratch, with those qubit-count formulas worked out explicitly on a small case you can picture completely.
